solution.concept_anchor: First Amendment 1951 — Articles 31A and 31B
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students familiar with zamindari abolition associate the 1st Amendment with land reform DPSPs and assume it must have altered Article 39, when in fact it left all existing DPSP text untouched.
elimination_logic: Eliminate any option suggesting the 1st Amendment altered the text of an existing DPSP article — its only DPSP-relevant action was inserting new Articles 31A and 31B.
Eliminate options linking the 1st Amendment to Article 31C — that article was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971), not the 1st.
Confirm that Article 31A protects estate-acquisition laws from Articles 14 and 19 challenges — this matches option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often assume that because the 1st Amendment was necessitated by zamindari abolition—a DPSP-driven policy—it must have modified the relevant DPSP articles (like Article 39). The trap is that 31A and 31B are not DPSP articles at all; they are inserted in Part III as shields against Fundamental Rights challenges. The 1st Amendment left every existing DPSP article completely unaltered.
solution.final_explanation:
The First Constitutional Amendment (1951) was passed after courts began striking down zamindari abolition laws on grounds of violating Articles 14 and 19. Parliament's response was to insert Articles 31A and 31B — both in Part III — to insulate land reform legislation.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971), not the 1st.
• Option (b): Correct. Article 31A shields laws relating to acquisition of estates from challenge under Articles 14 and 19; Article 31B gives the Ninth Schedule blanket protection.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The 1st Amendment did NOT alter any existing DPSP article. It added new provisions in Part III only.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Ninth Schedule was created by the 1st Amendment, but it was an entirely new schedule, not a replacement of any existing constitutional provision.

Value Addition:
• The immediate judicial trigger was State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952), though the amendment was enacted slightly before the judgment was delivered.
• The Ninth Schedule at creation contained only 13 entries; it now has 284.
• Post-IR Coelho (2007), Ninth Schedule laws inserted after April 24, 1973 can be reviewed for Basic Structure violations.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 31C scope — 25th vs 42nd Amendment fate

statement_analysis.statement: Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) to protect laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
statement_analysis.reason: The 25th Amendment's Article 31C in its original form shielded only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) — not all DPSPs — from Articles 14 and 19 challenge.

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Amendment expanded Article 31C's protection to all Directive Principles, and this expansion was struck down by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980).
statement_analysis.reason: The 42nd Amendment attempted to extend Article 31C to cover all DPSPs. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down this expansion as violating the Basic Structure doctrine.

statement_analysis.statement: After Minerva Mills (1980), Article 31C affords protection to laws implementing any of the Directive Principles of State Policy from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C protection is confined only to laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) — not all DPSPs — and does not extend to Article 21.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is the strongest distractor because students who recall that 42nd Amendment expanded 31C and that Minerva Mills struck it down may miss the precise error in Statement 3 regarding Article 21's inclusion.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 is correct — Article 31C as originally inserted by the 25th Amendment protected only 39(b) and (c) from Articles 14 and 19 challenges.
Confirm Statement 2 is correct — the 42nd Amendment expanded 31C to all DPSPs, and Minerva Mills (1980) invalidated this expansion.
Identify Statement 3 as incorrect — Article 31C never extended to Article 21, and post-Minerva Mills the protection remains limited to 39(b) and (c) only, eliminating options c and d.
The only combination with Statements 1 and 2 correct and Statement 3 incorrect is option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the trap: it contains 'any of the Directive Principles' (scope extension) and adds Article 21 to the shield, neither of which is accurate. A student who knows Minerva Mills reversed the 42nd Amendment's expansion may still mark Statement 3 as correct if they believe courts reading DPSPs into Article 21 means 31C protects Article 21 as well — a conflation of judicial interpretation with constitutional text.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31C is the central battlefield of the DPSP-Fundamental Rights conflict. Its journey across three amendments and two landmark judgments is a favourite UPSC theme.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C, shielding laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) from Articles 14 and 19 challenges. This original, limited protection survived judicial scrutiny.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 42nd Amendment (1976) expanded 31C to cover ALL DPSPs. The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down this expansion as destroying the constitutionally mandated balance between FRs and DPSPs — itself a Basic Structure element.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 31C never covered Article 21, and after Minerva Mills, the protection reverts strictly to 39(b) and (c) alone.

Value Addition:
• Kesavananda Bharati (1973) struck down the second part of original 31C (non-justiciability of DPSP laws), while Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the 42nd Amendment's expansion — two different surgical strikes on 31C.
• The 'balance' between FRs and DPSPs is itself a Basic Structure element per Minerva Mills.
• Only 39(b) and (c) — among all 20+ DPSPs — enjoy the Article 31C shield.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment — three new DPSPs 39A, 43A, 48A

statement_analysis.statement: Article 39A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, directs the State to ensure equal justice and provide free legal aid, and it forms the basis for the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 39A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment and explicitly directs equal justice and free legal aid; NALSA operates under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 founded on this DPSP.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 48A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment as a Directive Principle, has been used by courts to expand the right to life under Article 21 to include the right to a clean environment.
statement_analysis.reason: In Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991), the Supreme Court read Article 48A alongside Article 21 to hold that the right to a clean environment is a facet of the right to life.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 43A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, directs the State to ensure payment of a living wage and humane conditions of work to workers in industries.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 43A deals with workers' participation in the management of undertakings — not living wage, which is the subject of Article 43 (pre-existing DPSP).

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Statement 1 only incorrect) tempts students who are unsure whether 39A or a different article forms the NALSA basis, while missing the cleaner error in Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Article 39A is correctly described as equal justice/free legal aid and the basis for NALSA; Statement 1 is correct, so any option listing only Statement 1 as incorrect is eliminated.
Verify Statement 2 — Courts have indeed used 48A to expand Article 21 to include a clean environment (Subhash Kumar, 1991); Statement 2 is correct.
Identify Statement 3 as incorrect — Article 43A concerns workers' participation in management, NOT living wages; living wage is Article 43 which predates the 42nd Amendment.
Only Statement 3 is incorrect, pointing to option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 3 is an entity-swap between Article 43 (living wage — original DPSP) and Article 43A (workers' participation in management — inserted by 42nd Amendment). Both deal with labour welfare, making the swap very plausible. Students who remember '43A = 42nd Amendment = labour' may not recall the precise distinction between 'management participation' and 'living wage.'
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) was the most prolific amendment in terms of adding new DPSPs — it inserted Articles 39A, 43A, and 48A simultaneously.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 39A directs equal justice and free legal aid. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 and NALSA are direct legislative implementations.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 48A (environment protection as DPSP) has been judicially used to expand Article 21 to cover the right to a clean environment — a classic example of DPSP elevating a Fundamental Right's content.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 43A is about workers' participation in the management of industries. The living wage and humane conditions of work are directed by the pre-existing Article 43, inserted with the original Constitution.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment added the most DPSPs of any single amendment (39A, 43A, 48A) but simultaneously suffered the most judicial reversals (31C expansion, FR supremacy clause — both struck down).
• Article 51A(g) — Fundamental Duty to protect the environment — was also added by the 42nd Amendment, creating a DPSP (48A) + Duty (51A(g)) pair on the same subject.
• NALSA (National Legal Services Authority) constituted under Article 39A is frequently tested in context of access to justice.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment — right to property demotion to Article 300A

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Amendment deleted Article 19(1)(f) — the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property — from the list of Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment (1978) removed Article 19(1)(f) from Part III, eliminating the right to property as a Fundamental Right enforceable under Article 32.

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Amendment deleted Article 31 from the Constitution entirely, leaving no constitutional provision on the right to property.
statement_analysis.reason: While Article 31 was deleted from Part III, the 44th Amendment simultaneously inserted Article 300A in Part XII, preserving the right to property as a constitutional (not fundamental) right.

statement_analysis.statement: After the 44th Amendment, any law depriving a person of property must satisfy the test of reasonableness applicable to Fundamental Rights under Articles 14 and 19.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 300A only requires authority of law — it does not attract the strict reasonableness scrutiny applicable to Fundamental Rights; a person cannot move the Supreme Court under Article 32 for its violation.

statement_analysis.statement: Removing the right to property from Fundamental Rights reduced the primary source of conflict between Article 39(b) and (c) and property-related Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 were the principal Fundamental Rights against which DPSP Articles 39(b) and (c) clashed; their removal largely dissolved that specific tension.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (only two correct) tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 4 as correct but mistakenly accept Statement 2 (believing no replacement provision exists) or Statement 3 (confusing 300A's standard with FR scrutiny).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is clearly correct — 44th Amendment removed Article 19(1)(f) from Fundamental Rights.

Statement 2 contains a partial truth trap — Article 31 was deleted from Part III but Article 300A replaced it in Part XII, making 'leaving no constitutional provision' false; eliminate options that count Statement 2 as correct.
Statement 3 is incorrect — Article 300A does not attract FR-level scrutiny; the deprivation only requires legal authority, not reasonableness under Articles 14 or 19.
Only Statements 1 and 4 are correct — that is 'only two', pointing to option b... re-checking: options are (a) Only one, (b) Only two, (c) Only three, (d) All four. Two correct = option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the primary trap: students know Article 31 was 'deleted' and may not recall that Article 300A was inserted simultaneously as the replacement in Part XII. The phrase 'leaving no constitutional provision' is the false extension. Statement 3 is a secondary trap: it conflates the standard of review under Article 300A (authority of law) with the FR standard (reasonableness under Articles 14 and 19).
solution.final_explanation:
The 44th Amendment (1978) fundamentally reconfigured the right to property in India, reducing it from a Fundamental Right to a constitutional right — a downgrade with significant legal consequences.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 19(1)(f) was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 31 was removed from Part III, but Article 300A was simultaneously inserted in Part XII — the right to property continues to exist, just without Fundamental Right status.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 300A only requires that deprivation be under authority of law. It does not mandate the reasonableness test applicable under Articles 14 or 19. A writ under Article 32 does not lie for violation of 300A.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 were the main Fundamental Rights that clashed with DPSP Articles 39(b) and (c); their removal resolved much of that tension.

Value Addition:
• Right to property is now a constitutional right, meaning only High Courts (not Supreme Court) can be approached under Article 226 for its violation.
• The 44th Amendment was introduced by the Janata Party government — a political reversal of Indira Gandhi era amendments.
• Article 300A still provides that no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law — this protects against executive action without legal backing.

solution.concept_anchor: 86th Amendment — Article 45 revised scope after 21A insertion
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a pairs Article 45 (post-86th Amendment) with 'free and compulsory education for children up to 14 years,' which was its PRE-amendment content — a student who has not studied the amendment's effect on Article 45 will confidently choose this.
elimination_logic: Identify the post-86th Amendment content of Article 45 — it was changed to cover early childhood care for children BELOW 6 years, not 6–14.
Confirm Article 21A covers children aged 6–14 as a Fundamental Right — this eliminates any option that places 6–14 under Article 45 post-amendment.
Article 51A(k) — duty of parents to provide education — was added by the 86th Amendment alongside 21A; confirm this pairing.
The only combination consistent with these three facts is option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The critical trap is the post-amendment scope of Article 45. Before the 86th Amendment, Article 45 directed free and compulsory education for children up to 14 years. After the amendment, this was bifurcated: children 6–14 moved to Article 21A (Fundamental Right), while Article 45 was revised to cover early childhood care and education for children BELOW 6 years. Students who have memorised the original Article 45 without noting its amendment will mis-match it.
solution.final_explanation:
The 86th Amendment (2002) is the only amendment that simultaneously created a new Fundamental Right (Article 21A), amended an existing DPSP (Article 45), and added a new Fundamental Duty (Article 51A(k)).

Correct pairings:
• A–3: Article 21A provides free and compulsory education as a Fundamental Right for children between 6 and 14 years.
• B–1: Article 45 (post-86th Amendment) directs early childhood care and education for children BELOW 6 years — its earlier content (up to 14 years) was moved to Article 21A.
• C–4: Article 51A(k) — added by the 86th Amendment as a Fundamental Duty — makes it a duty of parents or guardians to provide education to their children between 6 and 14 years.
• D–2: The Right to Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) is the legislative implementation of Article 21A.

Trap pairing: A–1 is the classic error — placing the 6–14 age group under Article 45 (its pre-amendment content) instead of recognising that post-86th Amendment, Article 45 covers only under-6 children.

Value Addition:
• Before the 86th Amendment, the right to education for children up to 14 was judicially derived from Article 21 read with Article 45 (Unnikrishnan, 1993).
• The 86th Amendment is a rare instance where a DPSP's content was partially 'upgraded' to a Fundamental Right.
• Article 51A(k) is one of only two Fundamental Duties (along with 51A(j)) added by the 86th Amendment — the rest were added by the 42nd Amendment.

final_explanation:
The 86th Amendment (2002) restructured the constitutional framework on education by creating Article 21A, amending Article 45, and inserting Article 51A(k). Understanding the revised scope of Article 45 is the key examinable dimension.

Correct pairings:
• A–3: Article 21A provides free and compulsory education as a Fundamental Right for children aged 6–14 years.
• B–1: Article 45 (post-86th Amendment) covers early childhood care and education for children BELOW 6 years — it no longer covers the 6–14 age group.
• C–4: Article 51A(k), inserted by the 86th Amendment, casts a duty on parents/guardians to provide opportunities for education to children between 6 and 14 years.
• D–2: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) is the legislative operationalisation of Article 21A.

Trap pairings eliminated: A–1 and B–3 are the classic confusions — students pair Article 45 with the 6–14 age group because that was its original pre-amendment content.

Value Addition:
• Before 2002, Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993) derived the right to education from Article 21 read with Article 45 (DPSP) — a judicial bridge that the 86th Amendment later formalised.
• The 86th Amendment is the only amendment to simultaneously touch Part III (insert 21A), Part IV (amend 45), and Part IVA (insert 51A(k)).
• Children below 6 years remain under the DPSP framework — they cannot enforce their right to early childhood care under Article 32.

solution.concept_anchor: Champakam Dorairajan judgment triggering 1st Amendment
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b places Champakam Dorairajan after the 1st Amendment, which tempts students who know both events occurred in 1951 and may assume the Amendment preceded the judgment that 'prompted' it.
elimination_logic: The First Constitutional Amendment was enacted in June 1951 — BEFORE Champakam Dorairajan was decided by the Supreme Court; Parliament anticipated judicial invalidation based on the High Court order.
Champakam Dorairajan was decided by the Supreme Court in 1951 — after the 1st Amendment — making options placing it before the 1st Amendment incorrect.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) comes after both, and the 44th Amendment (1978) is the last in this sequence.
Correct sequence: 1st Amendment (1951) → Champakam Dorairajan SC judgment (1951, post-amendment) → Kesavananda Bharati (1973) → 44th Amendment (1978) — matching option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is that both Champakam Dorairajan and the 1st Amendment belong to 1951, so students assume the judgment caused the amendment in a neat cause-effect sequence. In reality, Parliament enacted the 1st Amendment first (June 1951) partly in anticipation of adverse judicial rulings on communal reservations, and the Supreme Court's Champakam judgment came after. The amendment added Article 15(4) to explicitly permit reservations for backward classes — overcoming the legal position the judgment had just confirmed.
solution.final_explanation:
The chronology of the early DPSP-Fundamental Rights conflict is a favourite UPSC theme because the 1st Amendment and Champakam Dorairajan both occurred in 1951, creating a counter-intuitive sequence.

Correct sequence:
1. First Constitutional Amendment (1951) — Added Articles 31A and 31B; also added Article 15(4) enabling state reservations for backward classes.
2. Champakam Dorairajan v. State of Madras — SC held that communal reservations in education violated Article 29(2); confirmed FRs prevail over DPSPs. This judgment arrived after the 1st Amendment.
3. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — Established Basic Structure doctrine; partially struck down Article 31C.
4. Forty-Fourth Amendment (1978) — Deleted Article 31 and Article 19(1)(f); inserted Article 300A.

Wrong options eliminated: Options placing Champakam before the 1st Amendment reverse the actual sequence. Options that insert the 44th Amendment before Kesavananda are also incorrect by fifteen years.

Value Addition:
• The 1st Amendment adding Article 15(4) is the earliest example of a constitutional amendment being used to 'nullify' the legal effect of a Supreme Court judgment.
• Champakam Dorairajan is the FIRST case where the Supreme Court explicitly held that Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs.
• The 44th Amendment was enacted under the Janata Party — the only non-Congress government to have made major constitutional changes up to that point.

Unnikrishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993): Right to Education Pre-86th Amendment

solution.concept_anchor: DPSP read into Article 21 — judicial enforceability technique
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Article 41 read with Article 21) is plausible because Article 41 mentions right to work, and students familiar with economic rights expansion may believe the Court used Article 41 rather than Article 39(a) in livelihood-deprivation cases.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves eviction of pavement dwellers who argue they have a right to livelihood — this maps directly to DPSP Article 39(a) (right to adequate means of livelihood) being read into Article 21.
Eliminate option a — Article 32 petitions relating to DPSP violations require the DPSP to be read into a Fundamental Right first; the scenario asks about the constitutional basis, not the remedy.
Eliminate option b — Article 41 (right to work) is a DPSP but the specific judicial principle in Olga Tellis used Article 39(a) read with Article 21, not Article 41.

Eliminate option c — Article 300A (right to property) relates to deprivation of property, not the right to livelihood; it also became relevant only after 44th Amendment and cannot be enforced under Article 32.
Option d correctly identifies the Olga Tellis principle: DPSP Article 39(a) read with Article 21 expands the right to life to include the right to livelihood.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b (Article 41 read with Article 21) is the intelligent distractor because Article 41 mentions 'right to work' which superficially resembles 'right to livelihood.' A student who has read about economic rights expansion under Article 21 but not the specific Olga Tellis judgment may choose this. The correct DPSP anchor is Article 39(a) — right to adequate means of livelihood — which the Court in Olga Tellis expressly used to expand Article 21's content.
solution.final_explanation:
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) is the landmark case establishing that the right to livelihood is a component of the right to life under Article 21. The judicial technique used was reading a non-justiciable DPSP into an enforceable Fundamental Right.

Applicable principle: Article 39(a) directs the State to ensure that citizens have adequate means of livelihood. Since DPSPs are not directly enforceable, the Court read Article 39(a) into Article 21 (right to life) to hold that life without the means to live is not 'life' in the constitutional sense. Eviction without alternative arrangements therefore violated Article 21 as expanded by Article 39(a).

Scenario mapping: The pavement dwellers' argument that eviction destroys their means of livelihood directly invokes the Article 39(a)+Article 21 principle from Olga Tellis.

• Option (a): Article 32 is the remedy provision — not the substantive principle justifying the claim.
• Option (b): Article 41 (right to work) was not the DPSP used in Olga Tellis — it was Article 39(a).
• Option (c): Article 300A protects against deprivation of property without legal authority — it is not about livelihood.
• Option (d): Correct — Article 39(a) read with Article 21 is the applicable constitutional principle.

Value Addition:
• Olga Tellis established the 'right to livelihood' as part of Article 21 — predating many other social rights expansions under Article 21.
• The same technique (DPSP + Article 21) was used in Subhash Kumar (1991) to derive the right to a clean environment from Article 48A.
• DPSPs, though non-justiciable independently, become enforceable when courts read them into Article 21 — this is the most significant judicial innovation in DPSP jurisprudence.

(b) Article 41 (right to work) read with Article 21 — since loss of livelihood is equivalent to deprivation of the right to work guaranteed by the Directive Principles
(c) Article 300A (right to property) read with Article 21 — since pavement dwellings constitute property and eviction without legal authority violates both provisions
(d) Article 39(a) (right to adequate means of livelihood) read with Article 21 — since the right to life includes the right to livelihood, and eviction without alternative arrangements violates this expanded right

concepts_used: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007): Ninth Schedule Judicial Review
Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981): Ninth Schedule and Post-Kesavananda Laws

solution.concept_anchor: Ninth Schedule — April 24 1973 cut-off for judicial review
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (a law inserted in the Ninth Schedule in 1979) tempts students who know the cut-off is the Kesavananda judgment date (1973) but are unsure whether 1979 is pre or post that threshold; they may second-guess whether the cut-off is the judgment date or the amendment date.
elimination_logic: The IR Coelho (2007) rule: Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule AFTER April 24, 1973 (date of Kesavananda judgment) are subject to Basic Structure review.
Laws inserted BEFORE April 24, 1973 retain absolute immunity per Waman Rao (1981).
Options a, b, and d all describe laws inserted after April 24, 1973 — all are subject to judicial review under IR Coelho.
Option c describes a law inserted in the Ninth Schedule in 1965 — before April 24, 1973 — making it the odd one out that retains absolute immunity.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the temporal precision required: the cut-off is not 1976 (42nd Amendment), not 1978 (44th Amendment), but April 24, 1973 — the specific date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment. A student who knows 'post-Kesavananda' but thinks of Kesavananda as '1970s generally' may wrongly include 1971 or 1974 laws in the reviewable category or exclude 1975 laws.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ninth Schedule immunity question turns on the April 24, 1973 cut-off established by Waman Rao (1981) and elaborated in IR Coelho (2007).

• Option (a): A land reform law inserted into the Ninth Schedule in 1976 — post April 24, 1973 — is subject to Basic Structure review per IR Coelho. Not the odd one out.
• Option (b): A law inserted in 1979 — post April 24, 1973 — is also subject to review. Not the odd one out.
• Option (c): A tenancy law inserted in the Ninth Schedule in 1965 — before April 24, 1973 — retains absolute immunity per Waman Rao. This is the odd one out — it CANNOT be reviewed for Basic Structure compliance.
• Option (d): A law inserted in 1981 — post April 24, 1973 — is subject to review. Not the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• The April 24, 1973 date is the exact date of delivery of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment — this precision matters in examination contexts.
• IR Coelho (2007) was decided by a nine-judge Constitutional Bench — the same numerical strength as Kesavananda.
• Even post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws are not automatically void — they are merely open to challenge on Basic Structure grounds; they do not lose immunity for other reasons.

solution.concept_anchor: 97th Amendment — cooperative societies, partial invalidation 2021

statement_analysis.statement: The Ninety-Seventh Constitutional Amendment (2011) simultaneously inserted a new Directive Principle (Article 43B on cooperative societies) and expanded a Fundamental Right (Article 19(1)(c) to include forming cooperative societies).
statement_analysis.reason: The 97th Amendment inserted Article 43B as a new DPSP on cooperative societies and amended Article 19(1)(c) to include the right to form cooperative societies as a Fundamental Right.

statement_analysis.statement: The entire Ninety-Seventh Constitutional Amendment was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India (2021) on the ground that it was passed without obtaining the consent of State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court in Rajendra N. Shah (2021) struck down only the PART of the 97th Amendment that dealt with state cooperative societies, holding it invaded states' domain without mandatory state ratification under Article 368(2). The provisions relating to multi-state cooperatives and the insertion of Article 43B were upheld.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both statements correct) is the strong distractor because Statement 2 contains accurate elements (the court did invoke Article 368(2) and did strike down portions) and students unfamiliar with the partial nature of the invalidation will accept it as fully correct.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — the 97th Amendment's dual action (Article 43B DPSP + Article 19(1)(c) expansion) is a well-established fact; Statement 1 is correct.

Identify the key flaw in Statement 2 — the phrase 'entire Ninety-Seventh Constitutional Amendment was declared unconstitutional' is the error; only the part relating to state cooperative societies was struck down.
The Supreme Court in Rajendra N. Shah upheld Article 43B and the multi-state cooperative provisions — confirming that Statement 2 overstates the judgment.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a 'partial-truth' trap: the Supreme Court DID strike down the 97th Amendment on Article 368(2) grounds AND DID hold that state ratification was needed — but only for the part concerning state cooperative societies. The word 'entire' makes Statement 2 false. Students who know the court struck down the amendment on ratification grounds may not recall that it was a partial striking down, leading them to mark both statements correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The 97th Amendment (2011) is notable for being simultaneously additive (new DPSP and expanded FR) and judicially curtailed (partial invalidation in 2021).

• Statement 1 — Correct: The amendment inserted Article 43B (promotion of cooperative societies as a DPSP in Part IV) and amended Article 19(1)(c) (adding the right to form cooperative societies as a Fundamental Right in Part III). This dual action across two Parts is rare.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court in Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India (2021) did NOT strike down the entire amendment. It struck down only those provisions dealing with STATE cooperative societies, holding that since cooperative societies fall in the State List (Entry 32, List II), Parliament needed to follow the special ratification procedure under Article 368(2) (ratification by not less than half the State Legislatures). Provisions relating to multi-state cooperatives and Article 43B survived.

Value Addition:
• This is one of the rare instances of a constitutional amendment being partially struck down — distinguishable from Minerva Mills (full sections struck down) by the federal-ratification ground.
• Entry 32 of the State List covers incorporation, regulation, and winding up of corporations other than those under the Union List.
• Article 43B remains a valid DPSP — promotion of cooperative societies is still a constitutional directive to the State.

solution.concept_anchor: 4th Amendment 1955 — expansion of Article 31A scope
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b attributes the expansion of Article 31A's scope beyond 'estates' to the 1st Amendment, which is the primary confusion the trap exploits — the 1st Amendment only covered estates originally, not the broader categories added in 1955.
elimination_logic: The 1st Amendment (1951) inserted Article 31A but limited its protection to laws relating to acquisition of 'estates'.
The extension of Article 31A's protection to management of properties, amalgamation of corporations, and extinguishment of rights was done by the 4th Amendment (1955).
Eliminate options attributing this expansion to the 1st Amendment — that is a temporal-swap trap.
Option a correctly identifies the 4th Amendment as expanding Article 31A's scope.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often associate all early land reform constitutional amendments with the 1st Amendment (1951) because zamindari abolition is the dominant narrative. The 4th Amendment (1955) is a less-recalled amendment that significantly expanded Article 31A's scope to include management of properties, amalgamation of corporations, and extinguishment of mining rights — categories well beyond 'estates.' Conflating the two amendments' contributions is the intended error.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31A's scope was not static at creation — it was significantly widened by the 4th Amendment.

• Option (a): Correct. The 4th Amendment (1955) expanded Article 31A beyond 'estates' to include laws relating to the taking over of management of properties, amalgamation of corporations, extinguishment of mining leases and other rights in minerals — insulating these additional categories from Articles 14 and 19 challenge.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The 1st Amendment (1951) inserted Article 31A — but its original scope was narrower, protecting principally laws relating to acquisition of estates from zamindars.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C — a different provision entirely. It did not expand Article 31A.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The 42nd Amendment added new DPSPs (39A, 43A, 48A) and expanded Article 31C — it did not alter Article 31A's scope.

Value Addition:
• 'Estate' in Article 31A's original form was defined to include jagirs, inams, muafi tenures, and similar grants.
• The 4th Amendment also added more zamindari abolition laws to the Ninth Schedule, reinforcing the shield from both the Article 31A route and the Ninth Schedule route.
• DPSP Article 39(b) and (c) provide the policy direction that Articles 31A and 31C seek to constitutionally protect in implementation.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 31C — only 39(b) and 39(c) among all DPSPs enjoy special shield

statement_analysis.statement: Among all the Directive Principles of State Policy, only Articles 39(b) and 39(c) enjoy the special constitutional protection under Article 31C that allows laws implementing them to override Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-Minerva Mills (1980), Article 31C's protection is confined strictly to laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) alone — no other DPSP enjoys this privilege.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024) unanimously held that 'material resources of the community' under Article 39(b) does not include privately owned resources under any circumstances.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court in Property Owners Association (2024) did not issue a unanimous ruling excluding all privately owned resources; the nine-judge bench reconsidered this issue and partially revisited earlier interpretations — the case involved a nuanced, non-unanimous position, not a categorical exclusion of private resources.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 39(c) directs the State to prevent concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment, and along with 39(b), forms the constitutional basis for nationalization laws.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 39(c) is precisely about preventing concentration of economic power, and together with Article 39(b), it forms the dual DPSP basis for laws on nationalization, land redistribution, and resource ownership restructuring.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (only Statement 1 incorrect) tempts students who are certain Statement 1 is accurate (it IS correct) but have not carefully read Statement 2's claim of 'unanimous' and 'under any circumstances' — both of which overstate the 2024 judgment.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C protects ONLY laws implementing 39(b) and (c); eliminate options listing Statement 1 as incorrect.

Statement 3 is correct — Article 39(c) is about preventing concentration of wealth, and both 39(b) and (c) underpin nationalization law jurisprudence; eliminate options listing Statement 3 as incorrect.
Statement 2 contains two false elements: 'unanimously' (the nine-judge bench in 2024 was not unanimous) and 'under any circumstances' (an absolute exclusion that the judgment did not endorse).
Only Statement 2 is incorrect → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the scope-extension trap by adding 'unanimously' and 'under any circumstances' — both of which make the otherwise plausible claim about privately owned resources being outside Article 39(b) incorrect. The 2024 Property Owners Association judgment is a recent and complex ruling that students may have read about but whose precise conclusions (partial overruling, not unanimous, not a categorical exclusion) are easy to mis-recall.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 39(b) and (c) occupy a unique position among DPSPs — they are the only ones with explicit constitutional protection under Article 31C to override Articles 14 and 19.

• Statement 1 — Correct: After Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the 42nd Amendment's expansion of Article 31C, only 39(b) and (c) retain the Article 31C shield. No other DPSP enjoys this.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024) nine-judge bench reconsidered the question of whether privately owned resources constitute 'material resources of the community' under Article 39(b). The bench partially revisited State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977) but did NOT unanimously hold that private resources are excluded under all circumstances — making both 'unanimously' and 'under any circumstances' factually incorrect.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 39(c) targets concentration of wealth and means of production. Together with Article 39(b)'s equitable distribution directive, they form the constitutional foundation for landmark nationalization legislation.

Value Addition:
• The 2024 Property Owners Association case is the most recent significant DPSP-related Supreme Court ruling and is relevant for current affairs segments in UPSC.
• Article 39(b) was interpreted broadly in State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977) to include privately owned resources — a position revisited in 2024.
• Nationalization of banks (1969) and insurance (1971) were legislative acts supported by Articles 39(b) and (c) alongside Article 31C.

solution.concept_anchor: Minerva Mills — balance between FRs and DPSPs as Basic Structure
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (both correct but R does not explain A) tempts students who are unsure whether the balance doctrine is the direct reason for striking down the 42nd Amendment's supremacy clause or merely a consequence stated alongside.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) factually correct? — Yes. In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court struck down the provision of the 42nd Amendment that attempted to give DPSPs supremacy over Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) factually correct? — Yes. The Court in Minerva Mills explicitly held that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself a part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The reason the Court struck down the 42nd Amendment's supremacy clause IS that making DPSPs superior to FRs would destroy the balance that is Basic Structure — R directly and causally explains A.
All three steps confirm option a: Both A and R correct, R explains A.
solution.final_explanation:
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) is the definitive case on the constitutional relationship between Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (Directive Principles). Its central holding is that neither set of provisions is absolutely superior — the balance between them is constitutionally mandated.

Assertion (A) analysis: The 42nd Amendment (1976) attempted to give DPSPs supremacy over Fundamental Rights by amending Article 31C to extend to all DPSPs and by inserting a provision that laws implementing DPSPs cannot be challenged on grounds of violating Articles 14, 19, and 31. The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills struck this down — this is what Assertion A correctly describes.

Reason (R) analysis: The Court's reasoning was precisely that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is a part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. Parliament cannot, through an amendment, tilt this balance so completely that Fundamental Rights become subordinate across the board to DPSPs — that would destroy an essential feature of the constitutional architecture.

Causal connection: R is the exact ground on which the Court struck down what A describes — making this a genuine option (a) scenario.

Value Addition:
• Minerva Mills also struck down Section 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which had made the amendment-making power of Parliament unlimited and immune from judicial review.
• The case reinforces that neither FRs nor DPSPs can be made absolute — constitutional harmony is the mandate.
• Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C protects only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) — its original, limited scope is restored.

solution.concept_anchor: Waman Rao vs IR Coelho — pre/post 1973 Ninth Schedule distinction

statement_analysis.statement: Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) confirmed that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973 are valid and cannot be challenged on any ground.
statement_analysis.reason: Waman Rao affirmed that the April 24, 1973 Kesavananda judgment date is the cut-off for Ninth Schedule immunity — pre-1973 insertions retain absolute protection.

statement_analysis.statement: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) was decided by a seven-judge Constitutional Bench and held that all laws in the Ninth Schedule, regardless of the date of insertion, are subject to judicial review.
statement_analysis.reason: IR Coelho was decided by a nine-judge bench (not seven), and it did NOT subject all Ninth Schedule laws to review — only those inserted AFTER April 24, 1973 are open to Basic Structure challenge.

statement_analysis.statement: The April 24, 1973 cut-off date for Ninth Schedule judicial review corresponds to the date on which the Kesavananda Bharati judgment was delivered by the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: April 24, 1973 is the specific date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment, which established Basic Structure — the cut-off is tied to this date because that is when the doctrine came into existence.

statement_analysis.statement: Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are automatically void and have no legal effect until reviewed by the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws are not automatically void — they are valid until challenged and struck down; the IR Coelho ruling only means they are OPEN to judicial review, not that they are presumed invalid.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (only two correct) is the strong distractor — students correctly identifying Statements 1 and 3 as correct may also mark Statement 2 as correct if they forget the bench strength (nine, not seven) and recall only the 'all laws subject to review' framing, which is also wrong.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Waman Rao confirmed absolute immunity for pre-April 24, 1973 Ninth Schedule insertions.
Statement 2 contains two errors: the bench was nine judges (not seven) AND the ruling does not cover all Ninth Schedule laws — only post-1973 insertions; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3 is correct — April 24, 1973 is indeed the Kesavananda judgment date and the cut-off.

Statement 4 is incorrect — post-1973 laws are open to challenge but not automatically void; Statements 1 and 3 correct = 'only two', option b... re-checking options: (a) Only one, (b) Only two, (c) Only three, (d) All four. Two correct = option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a temporal-swap trap (seven-judge vs. nine-judge bench) combined with a scope-extension (ALL Ninth Schedule laws vs. only post-1973 insertions). Statement 4 exploits the false inference that 'open to review' equals 'automatically void.' Students who recall IR Coelho as a landmark case may accept Statement 2's description without checking the bench composition or the precise scope of the ruling.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ninth Schedule judicial review question is governed by two landmark cases that address different temporal cohorts of laws.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Waman Rao (1981) held that laws in the Ninth Schedule inserted before April 24, 1973 retain absolute immunity from judicial review — they cannot be challenged on any constitutional ground.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: IR Coelho (2007) was decided by a nine-judge bench (not seven). More importantly, it did NOT subject all Ninth Schedule laws to review — only those inserted AFTER April 24, 1973 are open to Basic Structure challenge. Pre-1973 laws continue to have absolute immunity.
• Statement 3 — Correct: April 24, 1973 is the specific date the Kesavananda Bharati judgment was pronounced — the cut-off is tied to this date because Basic Structure doctrine came into existence then.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Post-April 24, 1973 Ninth Schedule laws are not automatically void. They carry a presumption of validity but are open to challenge — they become void only if a court strikes them down for violating Basic Structure.

Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — 'only two.'

Value Addition:
• The Ninth Schedule currently contains 284 entries — most additions came through amendments in the 1970s–1990s.
• IR Coelho (2007) is significant because it brought Constitutional Bench scrutiny back to the Ninth Schedule after decades of assumed absolute immunity.
• A petitioner challenging a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law must specifically argue Basic Structure violation — ordinary constitutional violations are not sufficient grounds.

solution.concept_anchor: Champakam Dorairajan — triggered 1st Amendment adding Article 15(4)
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Parliament added Article 31A to protect land reform laws) is plausible because Article 31A was added by the 1st Amendment, but it conflates the response to zamindari abolition cases with the response to Champakam — which specifically required Article 15(4) to permit reservations for backward classes.
elimination_logic: Champakam Dorairajan involved a state communal reservation in education that violated Article 29(2) — a Fundamental Right; the judgment held FRs prevail over DPSPs.
Parliament's specific response was to add Article 15(4) — enabling the State to make special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes — not to alter land reform provisions.
Eliminate option b — Article 31A protects zamindari abolition laws, not education reservations; this is an entity-swap between two different 1st Amendment additions.
Option d correctly identifies Article 15(4) as the provision added by the 1st Amendment in direct response to Champakam Dorairajan.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap uses an entity-swap: the 1st Amendment (1951) added both Article 31A AND Article 15(4), but they addressed different problems. Article 31A addressed judicial invalidation of zamindari abolition laws. Article 15(4) addressed Champakam Dorairajan's finding that communal reservations in education violated Article 29(2). A student who knows '1st Amendment = response to judicial invalidation' without distinguishing which provision responded to which case will incorrectly pick option b.
solution.final_explanation:
Champakam Dorairajan v. State of Madras (1951) held that a communal government order reserving seats in state medical and engineering colleges for different communities violated Article 29(2) — the right against denial of admission based on religion, race, caste, or language.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Article 16(4) (reservations in public employment) was an original constitutional provision and was not added by the 1st Amendment in response to Champakam.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Article 31A protects land acquisition laws from Articles 14 and 19 challenges — it was a response to zamindari abolition litigation, not educational reservation litigation.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Article 15(3) (special provision for women and children) is an original constitutional provision, not an amendment response to Champakam.
• Option (d): Correct. Parliament responded to Champakam by adding Article 15(4) through the 1st Amendment, enabling the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes or SCs/STs in educational institutions.

Value Addition:
• Champakam is significant as the first DPSP vs. FR conflict case — and the first instance of an amendment being used to overcome a Supreme Court judgment's legal effect.
• Article 15(4) later became the constitutional basis for OBC reservations in educational institutions.
• The 1st Amendment thus served a dual purpose: protecting zamindari abolition (via 31A, 31B) and permitting educational reservations (via 15(4)).

solution.concept_anchor: Right to education — judicial derivation 1993 vs explicit 21A in 2002

statement_analysis.statement: Prior to the Eighty-Sixth Amendment (2002), the Supreme Court in Unnikrishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) had already recognised the right to education for children up to 14 years as a Fundamental Right by reading Article 45 (DPSP) into Article 21.
statement_analysis.reason: In Unnikrishnan (1993), the Supreme Court held that the right to education up to the age of 14 is a Fundamental Right flowing from Article 21 when read with Article 45 — a judicial derivation that predates the 86th Amendment by nine years.

statement_analysis.statement: The Eighty-Sixth Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A and also inserted a new Directive Principle (Article 45) dealing with free and compulsory education for children up to 14 years, leaving Article 45's scope unchanged.
statement_analysis.reason: The 86th Amendment did not insert Article 45 — it AMENDED the pre-existing Article 45, changing its scope from children up to 14 years to early childhood care for children BELOW 6 years. Article 45 was already in the original Constitution.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Wait — option a is the correct answer. The strong distractor for students is option c (Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 correct) — students who know both the Unnikrishnan case and the 86th Amendment may accept Statement 2's description without noticing that Article 45 was amended (not newly inserted) and its scope was changed (not left unchanged).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Unnikrishnan (1993) did derive the right to education for under-14 children from Article 21 read with Article 45 DPSP before the 86th Amendment; Statement 1 is correct.

Examine Statement 2 carefully — it claims Article 45 was newly inserted by the 86th Amendment and that its scope was left unchanged; both sub-claims are false — Article 45 existed from 1950 and was AMENDED (not inserted) to cover under-6 children (not under-14).
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option c.
Recheck option mapping: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) Statement 1 correct Statement 2 incorrect, (d) Statement 1 incorrect Statement 2 correct → correct answer is c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a temporal-swap (implies Article 45 was inserted rather than amended) combined with a scope-extension error (claims scope unchanged when it was narrowed to under-6). Students who know the 86th Amendment added Article 21A and touched Article 45 may miss the critical distinction between 'amending existing 45' and 'inserting new 45', and may not recall that Article 45's age coverage was altered fundamentally.
solution.final_explanation:
The trajectory of the right to education — from DPSP to judicially derived right to explicit Fundamental Right — is a model example of how DPSPs evolve into enforceable rights.

• Statement 1 — Correct: In Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993), the Supreme Court read DPSP Article 45 (free education for under-14 children) into Article 21 (right to life) and held that the right to education up to age 14 is a Fundamental Right. This judicial derivation existed for nine years before Parliament formalised it.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 86th Amendment (2002) did NOT insert Article 45 — Article 45 was part of the original Constitution (1950). The Amendment MODIFIED Article 45, changing its content from 'free and compulsory education for children up to 14 years' to 'early childhood care and education for children below 6 years.' The scope was fundamentally altered, not left unchanged.

Value Addition:
• The 86th Amendment thus bifurcated the education mandate: children 6–14 → Article 21A (Fundamental Right); children below 6 → Article 45 (DPSP).
• Children below 6 cannot enforce their right to early childhood care under Article 32 — it remains a DPSP-level directive.
• The Right to Education Act, 2009 operationalises Article 21A and applies to children aged 6–14 years in formal schools.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The classic entity-swap in this question is placing Article 43B under the 42nd Amendment rather than the 97th Amendment. Since both deal with workers/labour/associations and the 42nd Amendment added Article 43A (workers in management), students conflate 43A (42nd Amendment) with 43B (97th Amendment). The 27-year gap between these amendments is the precise knowledge that separates a well-prepared student from one relying on surface associations.
solution.final_explanation:
Tracking which amendment added which DPSP is a foundational examination skill.

Correct pairings:
• A–2: Article 39A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — directs equal justice and free legal aid.
• B–4: Article 43B was inserted by the 97th Amendment (2011) — promotion of cooperative societies.
• C–3: Article 48A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) — protection of environment, forests, and wildlife.

Trap pairing: B–2 (placing 43B under 42nd Amendment) is the primary error — students conflate 43A (42nd Amendment) with 43B (97th Amendment).

Value Addition:

solution.concept_anchor: Article 43A — workers management participation not minimum wages
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Article 43A directs the State to secure payment of a living wage) is the most dangerous distractor because students confuse Article 43 (living wage — original DPSP) with Article 43A (workers' participation in management — 42nd Amendment). Both deal with labour welfare and the numbering proximity strengthens the confusion.
elimination_logic: Article 43A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment — this eliminates any option associating it with the original Constitution.
Article 43 (original DPSP) deals with living wage and humane conditions of work — 43A is a DIFFERENT provision on a different subject.
Article 43A specifically directs the State to take steps to secure participation of workers in the management of undertakings.
Option c correctly describes Article 43A as directing participation in management — not minimum wages, not social security.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap between Article 43 (living wage) and Article 43A (management participation) is a classic UPSC trap. Both articles share the same numbering root and both concern labour welfare, but they address entirely different aspects. Article 43 was part of the original Constitution; Article 43A was added 26 years later by the 42nd Amendment with a distinct mandate.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 43 and 43A are adjacent DPSPs that deal with different dimensions of worker welfare — confusing them is a common examination error.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The directive to secure a living wage, decent standard of life, and full enjoyment of leisure is in Article 43 — an original DPSP from 1950, not Article 43A.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Article 43A does not address social security or insurance for workers — those themes appear in other DPSPs and legislative acts.
• Option (c): Correct. Article 43A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976), directs the State to take steps to secure participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments, or other organisations engaged in any industry.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Equal pay for equal work is not the content of Article 43A — it is addressed indirectly through Article 39(d) and has been judicially read into Article 14 and 16.

Value Addition:
• Legislative implementation of Article 43A is visible in provisions for worker directors in public sector undertakings under the Companies Act.
• Article 43 (living wage) and Article 43A (management participation) together represent the dual aspiration for economic dignity and industrial democracy.
• The 42nd Amendment's three new DPSPs (39A, 43A, 48A) each have distinct legislative footprints: NALSA (39A), worker directors (43A), Environment Protection Act (48A).

solution.concept_anchor: Kesavananda — two distinct rulings on Article 31C

statement_analysis.statement: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court upheld the first part of Article 31C, which protects laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
statement_analysis.reason: The Court validated the first part of Article 31C as a legitimate legislative measure giving effect to DPSP 39(b) and (c) — this part survived judicial scrutiny.

statement_analysis.statement: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court struck down the second part of Article 31C which made laws implementing Directive Principles non-justiciable, holding that judicial review is a Basic Structure element.
statement_analysis.reason: The second part of original Article 31C purported to oust court jurisdiction over DPSP-implementing laws; Kesavananda held that judicial review cannot be excluded as it is part of Basic Structure.

statement_analysis.statement: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established that all Directive Principles of State Policy constitute part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution and cannot be abridged by any constitutional amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: Kesavananda did NOT hold that DPSPs form part of the Basic Structure. It held that Fundamental Rights (not DPSPs) are part of Basic Structure — and that the BALANCE between FRs and DPSPs is a Basic Structure element per Minerva Mills.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who know Kesavananda is a pro-constitutional landmark and associate it with protecting both FRs and DPSPs, incorrectly extending its holding to include DPSPs as Basic Structure elements.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Kesavananda upheld Article 31C's first part (39(b)/(c) shield from 14 and 19); Statement 1 is correct.
Confirm Statement 2 — Kesavananda struck down Article 31C's second part (non-justiciability clause) as violating judicial review which is Basic Structure; Statement 2 is correct.

Identify Statement 3 as incorrect — Kesavananda held Fundamental Rights (not DPSPs) are Basic Structure; it was Minerva Mills that said the BALANCE between FRs and DPSPs is Basic Structure — neither case made DPSPs themselves Basic Structure elements.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect → option b (1 and 2 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a partial-truth trap: students who know Kesavananda is associated with both DPSPs and Basic Structure may assume the Court protected DPSPs as Basic Structure. In fact, Kesavananda protected Fundamental Rights as Basic Structure. The separate proposition that the balance between FRs and DPSPs is Basic Structure comes from Minerva Mills (1980) — seven years later. Conflating the two cases' holdings is the intended error.
solution.final_explanation:
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) made two distinct rulings on Article 31C — one upholding it and one partially striking it down — which is often mis-stated in examinations.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Court upheld Article 31C's first part — that laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and (c) are protected from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. This represents the Court acknowledging that some DPSP implementation can validly override certain FR protections.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Court struck down Article 31C's second part — the declaration that such laws 'shall not be called in question in any court.' Judicial review is a Basic Structure element; Parliament cannot oust it even to implement DPSPs.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Kesavananda held that Fundamental Rights are part of the Basic Structure — not DPSPs. The proposition that the balance between FRs and DPSPs is Basic Structure was articulated later in Minerva Mills (1980). No Supreme Court judgment has held that DPSPs themselves are Basic Structure elements.

Value Addition:
• Kesavananda was decided by a 13-judge bench — the largest bench in Supreme Court history.
• The case overruled Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967), which had held Parliament had no power to amend Fundamental Rights.
• The 'Basic Structure' doctrine itself has no textual basis in the Constitution — it is entirely a judicial creation.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment — what was struck down vs what survived
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (expansion of Article 31C to all DPSPs) is the expected answer for students who know Minerva Mills struck down the 31C expansion — they may mark c as the 'odd one out' (the invalidated provision) while the question asks which provision was NOT struck down by the Supreme Court.
elimination_logic: The question asks which provision of the 42nd Amendment was NOT subsequently invalidated by the Supreme Court.
Expansion of Article 31C to all DPSPs → struck down in Minerva Mills (1980) — this WAS invalidated.
Provision giving DPSPs supremacy over Articles 14, 19, and 31 → struck down in Minerva Mills (1980) — this WAS invalidated.
Insertion of Article 39A (equal justice, free legal aid) → this was NOT struck down; it survives as a valid DPSP — this is the odd one out.
Non-justiciability clause in Article 31C's second part → struck down in Kesavananda (1973) — this WAS invalidated.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap is in the framing: the 42nd Amendment is famous primarily for what was struck down (31C expansion, DPSP supremacy clause), so students associate 'the 42nd Amendment' with invalidated provisions. Article 39A, also inserted by the same amendment, is entirely valid and has never been challenged. The question exploits this association by asking for the survivor among the invalidated provisions.
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) is unique in constitutional history — it simultaneously added valid DPSPs and inserted provisions that were subsequently invalidated by the Supreme Court.

• Option (a): The provision giving DPSPs supremacy over Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 — struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) as violating the Basic Structure (balance between FRs and DPSPs).
• Option (b): Insertion of Article 39A directing equal justice and free legal aid — this provision has NOT been invalidated and remains a valid, operational DPSP forming the foundation of NALSA and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. This is the odd one out.
• Option (c): Expansion of Article 31C protection to all Directive Principles — struck down in Minerva Mills (1980); only the original 39(b) and (c) protection survives.
• Option (d): The declaration in Article 31C making DPSP-implementing laws non-justiciable — struck down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment is sometimes called the 'mini-Constitution' because of its sweeping changes — but many were reversed.
• Article 39A's implementation through NALSA is a success story of DPSP-to-legislation conversion.
• The 42nd Amendment also added Article 51A (Fundamental Duties) — another provision that survived judicial scrutiny.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 31B Ninth Schedule — original intent vs post-IR Coelho review
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (A correct but R incorrect) tempts students who believe IR Coelho made ALL Ninth Schedule laws reviewable, which would make R's claim about pre-1973 absolute immunity incorrect — but pre-1973 laws DO retain absolute immunity, making R correct.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) factually correct? — Yes. Article 31B grants laws placed in the Ninth Schedule immunity from challenge on grounds of violating Fundamental Rights — this is its stated function.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) factually correct? — Yes. After IR Coelho (2007), laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule BEFORE April 24, 1973 retain absolute immunity — R is a correct and precise statement about the post-IR Coelho legal position.

Step 3: Does R causally or logically explain A? — Partially. R accurately describes the scope of 31B's immunity (what survived IR Coelho) but does not fully explain WHY 31B was created (which was to protect land reform laws from FR challenges). R explains the current limitation of 31B's immunity rather than its original rationale — the causal link between A's description of 31B's purpose and R's description of its post-IR Coelho scope is incomplete.
Both A and R are correct, but R describes the temporal limitation on 31B's immunity rather than causally explaining 31B's protective function — option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates in how R is constructed: it correctly describes that pre-1973 Ninth Schedule laws retain absolute immunity but adds 'this immunity was the original intent of Article 31B.' This conflates the original intent (protecting all Ninth Schedule laws from FR challenge) with what survived after IR Coelho (pre-1973 absolute immunity). R is factually correct as a statement about post-IR Coelho law but does not causally explain why Article 31B was inserted in 1951.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule operate as a shield — but one that was reshaped by judicial review over six decades.

Assertion (A) analysis: Article 31B, inserted by the 1st Amendment (1951), declares that none of the Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule shall be deemed void on the ground of being inconsistent with or taking away or abridging any of the rights conferred by Part III (Fundamental Rights). This accurately describes 31B's protective function.

Reason (R) analysis: After IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973 retain absolute immunity from judicial review. This is a correct statement about the current legal position — Waman Rao (1981) and IR Coelho (2007) together create this temporal bifurcation.

Causal relationship: R is factually correct but describes a consequence of IR Coelho's ruling on 31B's scope — not the original rationale for 31B's insertion. The 1st Amendment created 31B to protect zamindari abolition laws from all FR challenges; the pre-1973 absolute immunity is what survived after IR Coelho's judicial recalibration. R and A are both correct but R does not causally explain A's description of 31B's purpose.

Value Addition:
• The Ninth Schedule was created precisely because Parliament feared courts would strike down zamindari abolition laws — as they had begun to do before the 1st Amendment.
• IR Coelho's nine-judge bench is one of only three nine-judge benches in recent decades (others: Kesavananda and Property Owners Association 2024).
• Post-IR Coelho, a petitioner challenging a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law must demonstrate Basic Structure violation — not merely FR infringement.

solution.concept_anchor: DPSP-FR conflict — chronology of judicial and legislative responses
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b places Olga Tellis before Minerva Mills — students who associate both with the 1980s but have not fixed their sequence precisely may accept this order, especially since both deal with expanded Article 21.
elimination_logic: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) is the first event — the earliest DPSP-FR conflict case, predating all others.
Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971) — twenty years after Champakam; this is the second event.
Minerva Mills v. Union of India was decided in 1980 — after the 25th Amendment; third in sequence.
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation was decided in 1985 — after Minerva Mills; last in sequence. Correct order: Champakam → 25th Amendment → Minerva Mills → Olga Tellis = option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the Minerva Mills (1980) / Olga Tellis (1985) pair — both are 1980s Supreme Court cases and students often reverse their order. Additionally, students may misplace the 25th Amendment (1971) as either before or after Minerva Mills without fixing the precise year. The correct sequence requires fixing four events across four decades.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of the DPSP-Fundamental Rights relationship spans five decades of judicial and legislative action.

Correct sequence:
1. Champakam Dorairajan v. State of Madras (1951) — First DPSP-FR conflict case; Supreme Court held FRs prevail over DPSPs; directly triggered the 1st Amendment.
2. Twenty-Fifth Amendment inserting Article 31C (1971) — Parliament's attempt to give DPSP Articles 39(b) and (c) a constitutional shield against Articles 14 and 19; represented a partial legislative reversal of Champakam's principle for specific DPSPs.
3. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) — Supreme Court struck down 42nd Amendment's expansion of Article 31C; established the 'balance between FRs and DPSPs is Basic Structure' doctrine.
4. Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) — Supreme Court read DPSP Article 39(a) into Article 21 to derive the right to livelihood; demonstrated the judicial technique of DPSP-informed FR expansion.

Wrong options eliminated: Any option placing Minerva Mills after Olga Tellis reverses the 1980/1985 sequence. Any option placing the 25th Amendment before 1951 events is obviously incorrect.

Value Addition:
• The four events represent four distinct phases: judicial (1951), legislative (1971), judicial counter (1980), judicial expansion (1985).
• Each phase represents a different technique of managing the FR-DPSP relationship: conflict resolution, constitutional shielding, balance maintenance, and harmonious expansion.
• Olga Tellis (1985) is sometimes called the 'pavement dwellers case' and is a landmark in socio-economic rights jurisprudence.

solution.concept_anchor: 1st, 4th, and 25th Amendments — distinct contributions to land/DPSP law

statement_analysis.statement: The First Constitutional Amendment (1951) inserted Article 31A to protect estate acquisition laws from Articles 14 and 19, and also created the Ninth Schedule through Article 31B.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Article 31A (protection of estate acquisition laws) and Article 31B (creation of the Ninth Schedule) were inserted by the 1st Amendment simultaneously.

statement_analysis.statement: The Fourth Constitutional Amendment (1955) expanded Article 31A's protection to categories beyond 'estates', including laws relating to management of property and amalgamation of corporations.
statement_analysis.reason: The 4th Amendment extended the Article 31A shield to additional categories — management of properties, amalgamation of corporations, and extinguishment of mining rights — beyond the original estate-only protection.

statement_analysis.statement: The Twenty-Fifth Constitutional Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C and also amended Article 31A to include laws relating to nationalisation of industries within its protective scope.
statement_analysis.reason: The 25th Amendment inserted Article 31C — but it did not amend Article 31A. Nationalisation of industries is not added to Article 31A by the 25th Amendment; Article 31C operates independently as the shield for 39(b) and (c) laws.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 31B, inserted by the First Amendment, originally required Parliament to specify which laws were to be placed in the Ninth Schedule — it did not grant blanket immunity to all legislation dealing with land reform.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 31B protects only those laws specifically listed in the Ninth Schedule — not all land reform laws. Parliament must explicitly add a law to the Schedule for it to receive Ninth Schedule immunity.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (only three correct) is the strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statements 1, 2, and 4 as correct but accept Statement 3's false claim (that 25th Amendment also amended 31A) will mark 'only three' — missing that only the first, second, and fourth are correct while the third is wrong, still yielding 'only three'... wait, that IS three correct. Re-verify: Statements 1, 2, 4 are correct (three), Statement 3 is incorrect. 'Only three' = option c. Correct answer rechecked: c.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — 1st Amendment inserted both 31A and 31B simultaneously.
Statement 2 is correct — 4th Amendment expanded 31A beyond estates to management of property and amalgamation.
Statement 3 is incorrect — the 25th Amendment inserted 31C only; it did NOT amend 31A to include nationalisation; this is a false conflation of two distinct provisions.
Statement 4 is correct — Ninth Schedule immunity applies only to laws specifically scheduled, not all land reform laws; three of four correct = option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits a temporal-swap and conflation trap: the 25th Amendment DID insert Article 31C (which protects nationalisation-related laws implementing 39(b) and (c)), but students may confuse this with the 25th Amendment also amending Article 31A to include nationalisation. These are two separate provisions with separate scopes; the 25th Amendment's contribution was Article 31C alone.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1st, 4th, and 25th Amendments represent three distinct legislative interventions in the land reform/DPSP constitutional framework.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 1st Amendment (1951) inserted both Article 31A (protecting estate acquisition laws from Articles 14 and 19) and Article 31B (creating the Ninth Schedule). These two provisions operate differently — 31A is a substantive shield; 31B is a procedural listing mechanism.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 4th Amendment (1955) extended Article 31A's coverage to management of property, amalgamation of corporations, and extinguishment of mining rights — significantly broadening the range of laws that could override Articles 14 and 19.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C — a completely separate provision. It did NOT amend Article 31A. The two articles operate independently: 31A protects categories of laws specified in it; 31C protects laws specifically implementing Articles 39(b) and (c).
• Statement 4 — Correct: Ninth Schedule immunity under Article 31B applies only to laws Parliament explicitly places in the Schedule — blanket protection does not extend to all land reform legislation.

Three of four statements are correct → option c.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between 31A (category-based protection) and 31C (DPSP-linked protection) is a frequently tested conceptual pair.
• Laws can receive double protection — both by being within Article 31A's categories AND by being in the Ninth Schedule under 31B.
• The 25th Amendment's Article 31C is the constitutionally narrower provision; the 42nd Amendment tried unsuccessfully to broaden it.
