solution.concept_anchor: N.M. Thomas — Article 16(4) as facet not exception to 16(1)
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a ('an exception to the general rule of equality') is the classic pre-N.M. Thomas characterisation of Article 16(4) — students who have not specifically studied this case will naturally choose this formulation, which was the prevailing understanding before the judgment.
elimination_logic: The N.M. Thomas (1976) case specifically addressed whether Article 16(4) is an exception to Article 16(1) or something else.
The Court held Article 16(4) is NOT an exception but a 'facet' or 'application' of Article 16(1) — treating equality in substance rather than form.
Eliminate option a — 'exception' is the pre-N.M. Thomas characterisation that the judgment specifically rejected.
Eliminate options c and d — neither 'limitation' nor 'contradiction' reflects the Court's positive characterisation; option b ('facet') is the precise term used.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a ('an exception to Article 16(1)') was the legal orthodoxy before N.M. Thomas (1976) and remains the intuitive understanding for most students. The trap exploits this pre-existing intuition: students who have not specifically studied the N.M. Thomas holding will confidently select 'exception' because Article 16(4) does carve out a special category for backward classes, making it appear exception-like on the surface. The judgment's profound innovation was to recast this as a positive expression of equality rather than a departure from it.
solution.final_explanation:
N.M. Thomas (1976) reframed the constitutional understanding of the relationship between Article 16(1) (equality of opportunity in public employment) and Article 16(4) (reservations for backward classes).

• Option (a): Incorrect. 'An exception to the general rule of equality' was the pre-N.M. Thomas orthodox view — the judgment specifically rejected this characterisation.
• Option (b): Correct. The Supreme Court in State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas held that Article 16(4) is a 'facet' of Article 16(1) — it is not a departure from equality but an expression of substantive equality. Treating backward classes specially IS treating them equally in a material sense.
• Option (c): Incorrect. 'A limitation on the power of Parliament' mischaracterises Article 16(4) — it is an enabling provision (States MAY make reservations), not a limitation on Parliament.
• Option (d): Incorrect. 'A contradiction within the Constitution' is never an acceptable judicial characterisation of a constitutional provision.

Value Addition:
• N.M. Thomas (1976) pre-dates Indra Sawhney (Mandal Commission case, 1992) and laid the doctrinal groundwork for the facet/expression-of-equality view of reservations.
• The case established that implementing DPSP Article 46 (welfare of SCs/STs) through reservations harmonises with, rather than conflicts with, Article 16.
• Post-N.M. Thomas, Article 16(4) is understood as enabling backward class representation — a positive constitutional goal, not an exception to equality.

Forty-Second Amendment (1976): DPSP vs. Fundamental Rights — Supremacy Clause

solution.concept_anchor: DPSP amendability vs FR amendability — procedural and substantive limits

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike Fundamental Rights, which require a two-thirds majority plus majority of total membership and sometimes State ratification for amendment, Directive Principles of State Policy can be amended by a simple majority in Parliament and are therefore outside the scope of Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: DPSPs are part of the Constitution and must be amended under Article 368 — they are NOT amendable by simple majority. Article 368 requires a special majority (two-thirds of members present and voting plus majority of total membership) for all constitutional amendments, including those affecting DPSPs. The statement incorrectly conflates ordinary legislative majority with constitutional amendment procedure.

statement_analysis.statement: The Forty-Second Amendment's attempt to give Directive Principles supremacy over Fundamental Rights was struck down by the Supreme Court, establishing that the substantive balance between Part III and Part IV of the Constitution cannot be altered even through the Article 368 procedure.
statement_analysis.reason: In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court held that making DPSPs superior to FRs violates Basic Structure, meaning even the Article 368 special majority procedure cannot be used to destroy this balance — a substantive limitation on Parliament's amending power.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both statements correct) is the strong distractor because Statement 1 contains two separable claims — 'DPSP amendment requires different majority' and 'DPSPs are outside Article 368' — students who know DPSPs can be amended may not catch the false implication that they are outside Article 368 or require only simple majority.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — the claim that DPSPs are 'outside Article 368' and amendable by 'simple majority' is incorrect; all Parts of the Constitution including Part IV require the Article 368 special majority procedure for amendment.

Verify Statement 2 — Minerva Mills (1980) correctly described as striking down the 42nd Amendment's DPSP supremacy clause and establishing the substantive un-amendability of the FR-DPSP balance; Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct → option d.
Recheck option mapping: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) Statement 1 correct/Statement 2 incorrect, (d) Statement 1 incorrect/Statement 2 correct → answer is d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's scope-extension trap combines two elements: first, the true fact that DPSPs face fewer practical obstacles to amendment (no state ratification required, unlike some FR provisions); second, the false extension that this means they can be amended by simple majority or are outside Article 368. Many students know that 'DPSPs are easier to amend than FRs' and may extend this to 'DPSPs don't need the Article 368 procedure' — a significant overstatement.
solution.final_explanation:
The procedural and substantive limits on amending DPSPs versus Fundamental Rights is a nuanced topic that combines constitutional text with judicial doctrine.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: All constitutional provisions — including DPSPs in Part IV — must be amended through Article 368, which requires a special majority (two-thirds of members present and voting AND a majority of total membership of each House). Some FR amendments additionally require state ratification. DPSPs may require less frequent state ratification (most DPSP changes don't affect the lists requiring ratification) — but they are absolutely within Article 368's scope and cannot be amended by simple majority.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Minerva Mills (1980) established that Parliament cannot, even under Article 368, give DPSPs blanket supremacy over Fundamental Rights because the balance between Part III and Part IV is a Basic Structure element. This is a substantive limitation on the amending power — the special majority is a necessary but not sufficient condition.

Value Addition:
• Article 368 itself distinguishes between amendments requiring only special majority and those additionally requiring state ratification — but both categories require the special majority as a baseline.
• The Basic Structure doctrine adds a further substantive layer: even with the correct procedure, Parliament cannot amend certain features.
• Among constitutional scholars, there is no explicit provision declaring DPSPs easier to amend — the practical difference lies in which DPSP changes require state ratification (very few do).

solution.concept_anchor: Article 31C — protects only 39(b) and 39(c), not other DPSPs
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a pairs Article 31C with 'laws implementing all Directive Principles' — the trap exploits the 42nd Amendment's attempted expansion (which was struck down), making students who recall 'the 42nd Amendment tried to extend 31C' incorrectly believe it succeeded.
elimination_logic: Post-Minerva Mills (1980), Article 31C protects only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) — not all DPSPs.
Eliminate option a — 'all Directive Principles' was the 42nd Amendment's expansion, struck down in Minerva Mills; this pairing is incorrect.
Eliminate option b — Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971), not the 42nd Amendment (1976).

Eliminate option d — Article 31C is in Part III (as a modification to Article 31), not Part IV; option c correctly pairs Article 31C with its current operative scope (protecting 39(b) and (c) laws from Articles 14 and 19 challenge).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a exploits a conflation trap: the 42nd Amendment DID attempt to expand Article 31C to all DPSPs — and students who recall this expansion may assume it succeeded or that 'Article 31C = all DPSPs' is the current position. The Minerva Mills reversal is the key fact that defeats this assumption. Option b additionally conflates the inserting amendment (25th) with the expanding amendment (42nd), adding a temporal-swap layer.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31C's current operative scope is one of the most frequently examined facts in DPSP questions — and the conflation with the 42nd Amendment's failed expansion is a persistent source of errors.

• Option (a): Incorrectly paired. Article 31C does NOT protect laws implementing all Directive Principles — this was the 42nd Amendment's expansion, struck down in Minerva Mills (1980). The current scope is limited to Articles 39(b) and (c) only.
• Option (b): Incorrectly paired. Article 31C was inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment (1971), not the Forty-Second Amendment. The 42nd Amendment tried to expand its scope, not create it.
• Option (c): Correctly paired. Article 31C, in its post-Minerva Mills operative form, protects laws specifically giving effect to Articles 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 — this is the accurate and current constitutional position.
• Option (d): Incorrectly paired. Article 31C is not located in Part IV (DPSPs); it is inserted in Part III as a qualification to the operation of Fundamental Rights — placed after Article 31A and 31B.

Value Addition:
• Articles 39(b) and (c) are the ONLY DPSPs that enjoy Article 31C protection — uniquely privileged among all 20+ DPSPs.
• Article 31C's protection against Article 19 means laws implementing 39(b) and (c) cannot be challenged on grounds of unreasonable restrictions on property, trade, or profession rights.
• The 2024 Property Owners Association case reconsidered the scope of 'material resources' under 39(b) — showing this provision remains constitutionally live.

concepts_used: Champakam Dorairajan v. State of Madras (1951): First DPSP vs. FR Conflict
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Harmonious Construction Doctrine
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): Basic Structure and DPSPs

solution.concept_anchor: Three-case arc — Champakam to Kesavananda to Minerva Mills on FR-DPSP

statement_analysis.statement: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) established that in case of direct conflict, Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles — and this ruling was the only Supreme Court judgment to be immediately 'overcome' by a constitutional amendment that added a new Fundamental Rights clause (Article 15(4)).
statement_analysis.reason: Champakam is correctly described as the first FR-DPSP conflict case; and Article 15(4) added by the 1st Amendment is correctly characterised as a constitutional amendment responding to a Supreme Court judgment by adding to Part III itself — this is historically unique.

statement_analysis.statement: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights is unrestricted as long as the amendment serves the objectives set out in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
statement_analysis.reason: Kesavananda held the opposite — Parliament's amending power is LIMITED by the Basic Structure doctrine; amendments cannot destroy essential features even if intended to implement DPSPs. The case overruled the unlimited amendment power view from Golak Nath was being contested.

statement_analysis.statement: Minerva Mills (1980) held that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself part of the Basic Structure, meaning Parliament cannot tip the constitutional scales entirely in favour of either Part III or Part IV.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise holding of Minerva Mills — the harmony between the two sets of provisions is constitutionally mandated and cannot be destroyed by any amendment, making neither part absolutely dominant.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who know all three cases are major FR-DPSP milestones and accept Statement 2's description without noting that Kesavananda established LIMITS on amending power — not unlimited power with a DPSP-purpose qualification.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Champakam is correctly described, and Article 15(4) being added to Part III (not Part IV) in response to a Part III ruling is indeed historically unique; Statement 1 is correct.

Identify the fundamental error in Statement 2 — Kesavananda held Parliament's amending power has LIMITS (Basic Structure); it did NOT hold that DPSP-motivated amendments are unrestricted; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — Minerva Mills' holding that the FR-DPSP balance is Basic Structure is precisely stated; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option a (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap: Kesavananda IS associated with DPSPs (it upheld the first part of Article 31C), and students may construct a connection between DPSP-motivated amendments and parliamentary power. The statement sounds reasonable — 'Parliament can amend FRs if it's for DPSPs' — but this is exactly the position Minerva Mills (1980) rejected, building on Kesavananda's Basic Structure constraint.
solution.final_explanation:
The three-case arc from Champakam (1951) to Kesavananda (1973) to Minerva Mills (1980) represents the complete judicial evolution of the FR-DPSP relationship.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Champakam established FR supremacy over DPSPs in 1951. Parliament responded with the 1st Amendment adding Article 15(4) — a new clause within Part III (Fundamental Rights) itself, not a DPSP. This is unique: a judgment on Part III was overcome by adding to Part III rather than amending Part IV.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Kesavananda established LIMITS on Parliament's amending power through Basic Structure — it did not grant Parliament unlimited amending authority for DPSP purposes. The Basic Structure doctrine means some features cannot be destroyed even by DPSP-motivated amendments.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Minerva Mills synthesised Kesavananda's Basic Structure constraint with the DPSP framework by holding that the balance between Part III and Part IV is itself Basic Structure — neither can be made absolutely superior to the other.

Value Addition:
• The 1st Amendment's addition of Article 15(4) to Part III is the only instance of a constitutional amendment 'defeating' a Supreme Court judgment by expanding the very Part the Court had applied.
• Kesavananda's thirteen-judge bench included Chief Justice Sikri — retired the same day the judgment was delivered, which was also his last day in office.
• Minerva Mills (1980) also struck down Section 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which had made Parliament's amending power immune from judicial review — doubly reasserting Basic Structure.

solution.concept_anchor: DPSP-related amendments — matching amendment to its unique constitutional feature
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a swaps the 86th and 97th Amendment descriptions — students who know both involve dual-category changes (FR + DPSP) but don't distinguish which amendment amended an existing DPSP (86th) versus added a new one (97th) will choose a.
elimination_logic: The 42nd Amendment is uniquely known for adding three new DPSPs AND having its supremacy provisions struck down — no other amendment matches this dual profile.

The 86th Amendment AMENDED an existing DPSP (Article 45) — narrowing its scope and simultaneously creating Article 21A as a new FR; the amendment changed the content of an existing DPSP rather than adding a new one.
The 97th Amendment added a new DPSP (Article 43B) AND expanded an existing FR (Article 19(1)(c)) AND was partially struck down in 2021 — this three-feature profile matches List II item 4.
The 25th Amendment inserted Article 31C alone — no new DPSP was added; it was a shield provision. This matches List II item 1. Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4 = option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap between the 86th and 97th Amendments is the primary trap: both involved simultaneous changes to FRs and DPSPs. The distinction is that the 86th Amendment AMENDED (narrowed) an existing DPSP (Article 45), while the 97th Amendment ADDED a new DPSP (Article 43B). Additionally, only the 97th Amendment was partially struck down. Students who blur these distinctions will misplace the amendments in List II.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing the constitutional features of each major DPSP-related amendment requires precise knowledge of what each amendment added, changed, and what judicial fate it met.

Correct pairings:
• A (42nd Amendment, 1976) — 3: Added three new DPSPs (39A, 43A, 48A) — the maximum added by any single amendment — while simultaneously attempting (unsuccessfully) to give DPSPs supremacy over FRs.
• B (25th Amendment, 1971) — 1: Inserted Article 31C alone — a shield for laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c); did not add any new DPSP article to Part IV.
• C (86th Amendment, 2002) — 2: Amended the existing Article 45 (DPSP) to cover only under-6 children while inserting Article 21A (FR) for children aged 6–14 — uniquely amended an existing DPSP's scope.
• D (97th Amendment, 2011) — 4: Added Article 43B (new DPSP) + expanded Article 19(1)(c) (FR) + was partially struck down in Rajendra N. Shah (2021) for state cooperative society provisions.

Trap pairings: C–4 and D–2 are the expected swaps — students confuse which amendment involved partial judicial invalidation and which amended an existing DPSP.

Value Addition:
• No other constitutional amendment has combined adding a new FR, amending an existing DPSP, and adding a new Fundamental Duty in a single act — the 86th Amendment did all three.
• The 97th Amendment's partial invalidation in 2021 is the most recent major DPSP-related judicial decision.
• The 25th Amendment's Article 31C was judicially modified twice — first by Kesavananda (1973) and then indirectly by Minerva Mills (1980).

solution.concept_anchor: DPSP enforcement technique — reading into FRs not direct enforcement

statement_analysis.statement: In Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993), the Supreme Court held that because Article 45 (DPSP) is non-justiciable, the right to education cannot be recognised as enforceable in any form prior to a constitutional amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: Unnikrishnan (1993) held exactly the opposite — the Court derived the right to education for under-14 children as a Fundamental Right by reading Article 45 INTO Article 21, creating an enforceable right without a constitutional amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: N.M. Thomas (1976) demonstrated that DPSPs can inform the INTERPRETATION of Fundamental Rights, enabling a court to read a Fundamental Right provision more broadly to accommodate DPSP objectives.
statement_analysis.reason: N.M. Thomas used DPSP Article 46 to inform the interpretation of Article 16(1) — holding that substantive equality (giving effect to 46) is consistent with Article 16(1)'s equality mandate, demonstrating the interpretive role of DPSPs.

statement_analysis.statement: The judicial technique of reading DPSPs into Article 21 to expand the right to life was first employed in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), using Article 39(a) to include the right to livelihood within Article 21.
statement_analysis.reason: Olga Tellis (1985) is indeed credited with pioneering the Article 39(a)+Article 21 reading to derive the right to livelihood — it is among the earliest applications of this technique to a socio-economic DPSP.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Statement 2 only incorrect) is the strong distractor because Statement 2 correctly describes N.M. Thomas and students who know this case will confidently mark Statement 2 as correct — but they must also identify Statement 1 as incorrect (it reverses the Unnikrishnan holding).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 contains a reversed-causation error — Unnikrishnan did NOT hold that DPSP non-justiciability prevents any right derivation; it did the opposite, deriving the right to education via Article 21+45.
Statement 2 is correct — N.M. Thomas is precisely about DPSPs informing FR interpretation.
Statement 3 is correct — Olga Tellis pioneered the Article 39(a)+21 technique for the right to livelihood.
Only Statement 1 is incorrect → option d (Statement 1 only NOT correct).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a reversed-causation trap: the statement implies that because DPSPs are non-justiciable, a court must wait for a constitutional amendment before recognising any DPSP-grounded right. But Unnikrishnan (1993) did the reverse — it used the non-justiciable DPSP (Article 45) as interpretive material to EXPAND a Fundamental Right (Article 21), creating an enforceable right without any constitutional amendment. This reversal of the judicial technique is the core error.
solution.final_explanation:
The three cases in this question represent the sophisticated judicial toolkit for making DPSP objectives practically enforceable without amending the Constitution.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Unnikrishnan v. State of AP (1993) held that the right to education for children up to 14 years IS a Fundamental Right — derived from Article 21 read with Article 45 (DPSP). The Court did NOT hold that non-justiciability of 45 bars any enforceable right before a formal amendment. The statement completely reverses the judgment's holding.
• Statement 2 — Correct: N.M. Thomas demonstrated the interpretive role of DPSPs — Article 46 (welfare of SCs/STs) was used to read Article 16(1)'s equality mandate substantively, enabling reservations to coexist with equality rather than conflict with it.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Olga Tellis (1985) is the landmark case for the Article 39(a)+Article 21 technique. By holding that life without means of livelihood is not 'life' in the constitutional sense, the Court enforcibly embedded a DPSP objective within a Fundamental Right.

Only Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Value Addition:
• The three judicial techniques — reading DPSPs into FRs (Olga Tellis), using DPSPs to interpret FRs (N.M. Thomas), and DPSP+Article 21 derivation (Unnikrishnan) — together constitute India's 'social rights jurisprudence.'
• Post-86th Amendment (2002), the Unnikrishnan judicial derivation was formalised as Article 21A — showing how judicial creativity eventually becomes constitutional text.
• The non-justiciability of DPSPs (Article 37) is therefore not an absolute barrier — it prevents direct enforcement through writs but not indirect enforcement via FR interpretation.

First Amendment (1951): Addition of Article 31A and 31B

solution.concept_anchor: IR Coelho — post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws and Basic Structure review
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct, R explains A) tempts students who accept both A and R as true facts and assume that because both involve Ninth Schedule review, they must be causally connected — without scrutinising whether R specifically explains WHY A's principle applies.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) factually correct? — Yes. After IR Coelho (2007), laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 can be challenged if they violate Fundamental Rights that are part of the Basic Structure.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) factually correct? — Yes. The Waman Rao (1981) ruling that pre-April 24, 1973 insertions have absolute immunity is a correct statement of law.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. R describes the immunity of PRE-1973 laws; A describes the reviewability of POST-1973 laws. These are complementary but not causally connected — R's statement about pre-1973 immunity does not EXPLAIN why post-1973 laws are reviewable. The reason for A is that Kesavananda established Basic Structure on April 24, 1973, not that pre-1973 laws are immune.
Both A and R are correct, but R does not explain A → option b.
solution.final_explanation:
The IR Coelho (2007) framework creates a temporal bifurcation in Ninth Schedule immunity, and it is important to understand the causal logic rather than just the factual outcomes.

Assertion (A) analysis: IR Coelho held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 — the date of the Kesavananda judgment — can be judicially reviewed if they violate Fundamental Rights forming part of the Basic Structure. This is because once the Basic Structure doctrine came into existence, any subsequent constitutional action (including Ninth Schedule insertions) is subject to it.

Reason (R) analysis: Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) confirmed that pre-April 24, 1973 Ninth Schedule insertions retain absolute immunity. This is also correct — Waman Rao and IR Coelho together create the temporal divide.

Causal relationship: R describes the immunity of pre-1973 laws. A describes the reviewability of post-1973 laws. The reason post-1973 laws are reviewable is NOT that pre-1973 laws are immune — that would reverse the causation. The actual reason for A is the emergence of the Basic Structure doctrine on April 24, 1973: any law placed in the Ninth Schedule after that date cannot claim immunity against Basic Structure violation. R and A are complementary facts, but R does not causally explain A.

Value Addition:
• The April 24, 1973 cut-off is the most precise date in DPSP/Ninth Schedule jurisprudence — worth memorising exactly.
• IR Coelho did not strike down any specific Ninth Schedule law — it only established the principle of reviewability for post-1973 insertions.
• A petitioner challenging a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law must specifically demonstrate that the law violates a Fundamental Right that constitutes part of the Basic Structure.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 300A — constitutional right to property, enforceable via HC not SC
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d ('a person can approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 for violation of Article 300A since it is a constitutional right') is the most dangerous distractor because students who know Article 300A is a constitutional right may infer that it can be enforced through the Supreme Court — forgetting that Fundamental Right status is the prerequisite for Article 32 jurisdiction.
elimination_logic: The key distinction is between a Fundamental Right (Part III, Article 32 enforceable) and a constitutional right (Article 300A, only Article 226 enforceable).
Article 300A is not in Part III — it is in Part XII; therefore Article 32 does not apply to its violation.
A person can approach a High Court under Article 226 for violation of Article 300A — not the Supreme Court under Article 32.
Eliminate option d (Article 32 available) — only Article 226 lies; option c correctly states this distinction.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option d exploits a scope-extension: students who know '300A = constitutional right = legally protected' may extend this to 'constitutional right = Supreme Court enforceable under Article 32.' The error is that Article 32 is available ONLY for Fundamental Rights violations — its entire jurisdictional basis is Article 13's definition of Fundamental Rights in Part III. Article 300A, being in Part XII, does not trigger Article 32 jurisdiction.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 300A is the post-44th Amendment home of the right to property — a carefully calibrated demotion from Fundamental Right to constitutional right.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The right to property under Article 300A requires 'authority of law' — not 'public purpose and compensation' as applicable under the erstwhile Article 31. The substantive standard is lower than what applied to the Fundamental Right to property.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The 44th Amendment deleted Article 31 from Part III AND deleted Article 19(1)(f). Article 300A was inserted simultaneously as the replacement — no provision was left untouched.
• Option (c): Correct. Since Article 300A is not part of Part III (Fundamental Rights), Article 32 of the Constitution — which provides for Supreme Court remedies for FR violations — does not apply. A person whose property is taken without legal authority must petition the High Court under Article 226.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Article 32 jurisdiction is limited to Fundamental Rights. Article 300A is explicitly placed outside Part III and therefore beyond Article 32's reach.

Value Addition:
• The practical significance: Property deprivation without legal authority can be challenged in HC (Article 226) but NOT in SC (Article 32) — a jurisdictional difference with real litigation implications.
• Article 300A's standard ('save by authority of law') protects only against executive action; a law duly passed can authorise property deprivation without compensation.
• The removal of Article 31 eliminated the constitutional requirement of compensation for property acquisition — a major policy shift in land reform and nationalisation.

(d) A person can approach the Supreme Court directly under Article 32 for violation of Article 300A since it remains a constitutionally guaranteed right even after the Forty-Fourth Amendment

The governing principle after Minerva Mills (1980) is harmonious construction — courts should read FRs and DPSPs together rather than making one absolutely superior.
Eliminate option a (Article 19 automatically prevails) — this is the pre-42nd Amendment Champakam orthodoxy, which Minerva Mills qualified by establishing the balance as Basic Structure.

Students who know Article 31C is relevant to DPSP-FR conflicts may accept this broad formulation without recalling that Minerva Mills confined the shield to 39(b) and (c) only. The scenario's law may implement a different DPSP, making option c inapplicable.
solution.final_explanation:
When a law implementing a Directive Principle is challenged on grounds of violating a Fundamental Right, the governing judicial doctrine — post Minerva Mills (1980) — is harmonious construction.

Applicable principle: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court held that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself part of the Basic Structure. Courts are therefore required to read the two sets of provisions harmoniously — neither should be made absolutely superior. This is the doctrine of harmonious construction applied at the constitutional level.

Scenario mapping: A law implementing a DPSP (labour welfare) challenged under Article 19 (freedom to carry on trade or business) should be examined for whether a harmonious reading of both provisions is possible — whether the restriction on Article 19 is reasonable in light of DPSP objectives, rather than automatically invalidating the law or automatically upholding it.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Article 19 does not automatically prevail — that was Champakam's (1951) pre-42nd Amendment position, later qualified by Minerva Mills.
• Option (b): Correct. Harmonious construction — reading FRs and DPSPs together to give effect to both where possible — is the Minerva Mills doctrine.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Article 31C protects only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) from Articles 14 and 19. It does not shield all DPSP laws from all FR challenges.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The 42nd Amendment's DPSP supremacy provision was struck down in Minerva Mills — DPSPs do not automatically prevail over FRs.

Value Addition:
• Harmonious construction is the 'preferred reading' in constitutional interpretation — courts avoid conflict between constitutional provisions by reading them together.
• The Minerva Mills balance principle is now the bedrock doctrine: neither FRs nor DPSPs can be made absolute at the other's expense.
• Only if harmonious construction is impossible — genuine irreconcilable conflict — would a court invoke the residual FR precedence from pre-Minerva Mills doctrine.

A State legislature enacts a law that mandates compulsory representation of workers on the board of management of large private sector enterprises, implementing a Directive Principle of State Policy on workers' participation in industrial management. A business association challenges the law before a constitutional court, arguing that it violates their right to carry on business freely under Article 19. The law does not involve distribution of material resources and is not specifically covered under Article 31C. Which of the following most accurately describes the approach a constitutional court would adopt, consistent with the current constitutional position?

(a) The court must strike down the law because Article 19 is a Fundamental Right and automatically prevails over any Directive Principle that conflicts with it, in accordance with the principle established in Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
(b) The court must attempt to harmoniously construct the Directive Principle and the Fundamental Right, recognising that neither Part III nor Part IV is absolutely superior, and uphold the law if it imposes only a reasonable restriction on Article 19 in furtherance of a public interest objective
(c) The court must uphold the law because Article 31C protects any legislation that implements a Directive Principle of State Policy from challenge under Article 19, regardless of which specific DPSP is involved
(d) The court must uphold the law because the Forty-Second Amendment gave Directive Principles supremacy over Fundamental Rights, making legislative action implementing DPSPs immune from Article 19 challenge

solution.final_explanation:
Matching DPSP articles to their inserting/amending amendments is a core factual skill for this topic.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) alongside Articles 43A and 48A.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 43B (promotion of cooperative societies) was inserted by the 97th Amendment (2011) — NOT the 86th Amendment (2002). The 86th Amendment's DPSP contribution was amending Article 45 (not inserting a new article).
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 48A (environment and forest protection) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
• Statement 4 — Correct: The 86th Amendment (2002) amended the pre-existing Article 45 to change its coverage from children 'up to 14 years' to children 'below 6 years' — with the 6–14 group covered by the newly inserted Article 21A (Fundamental Right).

Three of four statements are correct → option c.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment (1976) trio: 39A (legal aid), 43A (management participation), 48A (environment) — remember as LAM (Legal Aid, Management, Environment).
• The 86th Amendment's DPSP action was AMENDING 45 — not inserting a new DPSP; a distinction that appears in examinations.
• The 97th Amendment (2011) added Article 43B — cooperative societies — and this is the most recent DPSP article to be added by amendment.
